gaps.sentence: Visitors ___ leave any bags unattended; security removes them at once.
gaps.explanation: 'Must not' expresses prohibition; 'need not' would mean it is optional.

gaps.sentence: It ___ be the postman — he has already been this morning.
gaps.hint: ruled out by what already happened
gaps.explanation: Evidence that rules something out uses 'can't': can't be.

gaps.sentence: Visitors ___ to leave the gallery by 6 p.m.
gaps.hint: have to takes the full infinitive
gaps.explanation: 'Have to' takes the full infinitive with 'to': have to leave.

gaps.sentence: I ___ rather stay in tonight, if that's all right.
My grandmother ___ speak five languages, but she has forgotten most of them.
gaps.explanation: 'Could' expresses general past ability: could speak.

gaps.sentence: After three attempts, she ___ pass her driving test at last.
gaps.explanation: A specific past success takes 'was able to' or 'managed to': was able to pass.

gaps.sentence: You ___ bring your own laptop — we will provide everything.
gaps.hint: no obligation, so needn't not mustn't
gaps.explanation: 'Needn't' means it is not necessary; 'mustn't' would mean it is prohibited: needn't bring.

gaps.sentence: She ___ to pass one more exam to qualify as an architect.
gaps.explanation: 'Need to' conjugates like a normal verb: she needs to pass.
